meta.title: Who really said "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it's Rousseau. The opening line of The Social Contract (1762). The elegant English is the translator's; Rousseau wrote it in French.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Rousseau — the opening sentence of The Social Contract (1762). The familiar English is G. D. H. Cole's 1913 rendering of the French original.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the celebrated opening sentence of Rousseau’s “Du contrat social” (The Social Contract), 1762, Book I, ch. 1. Rousseau wrote it in French — “L’homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers” — and the familiar English phrasing is a translator’s rendering, most often G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 version (which uses a semicolon; the comma is a common later variant).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Book I, Chapter 1 — “Subject of the First Book”
English wording from G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 translation

source.excerpt: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains. One thinks himself the master of others, and still remains a greater slave than they. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.
trail: The line opens Book I, ch. 1 of Rousseau’s “Du contrat social” (1762); Wikiquote records the French original and the Cole rendering in its sourced entry.
G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 translation reads “Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains,” as reproduced in the Marxists Internet Archive text.
The popular comma form (“Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains”) is a punctuation variant of the same sentence; the words are Rousseau’s via his translators.
source.excerptNote: G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 English translation. Rousseau’s French original: “L’homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers. Tel se croit le maître des autres, qui ne laisse pas d’être plus esclave qu’eux.”

source.rightsNote: Rousseau’s French original was first published in 1762 and is long in the public domain. The specific English wording shown is G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 translation, also published before 1931 and therefore in the public domain in the United States.

author.heading: About Jean-Jacques Rousseau
author.metaLine: 1712–1778 · Genevan philosopher, writer & composer of the Enlightenment
author.bio: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Geneva-born philosopher whose political and educational writings helped shape the French Revolution and modern democratic thought. Du contrat social (1762) argued that legitimate political authority rests on a “general will” agreed by the people. Its opening line became one of the most quoted sentences in all of political philosophy.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Rousseau is correct — this really does open The Social Contract. The confusion is about the exact words, since Rousseau wrote in French and the memorable English belongs to his translators.

items.why: Rousseau wrote “L’homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers.” The polished English — “Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains” — is G. D. H. Cole’s 1913 translation; other renderings use “shackles” or “bondage.”
The widely shared comma form (“Man is born free, and everywhere…”) and the “Man was born free” variant differ slightly from Cole’s semicolon original, as the Wikiquote entry shows.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the sentence are genuinely Rousseau’s, from the opening of The Social Contract (1762) — only the English phrasing is a translator’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Rousseau opens The Social Contract with a paradox: humans are naturally free, yet live everywhere under constraint. The rest of the book asks not how to break every chain, but how political authority can be made legitimate — grounded in the consent and “general will” of the people rather than force.
The sentence became a rallying phrase in the French and later revolutions, and remains a touchstone in debates about freedom, authority, and the state.
